title: Why infrastructure as code
summary: What goes wrong when infrastructure is clicked together by hand, declarative versus imperative tools, and your first init, plan and apply.

steps.title: Clicking it together does not scale
body: Most companies start by creating servers, databases and DNS records by hand in a cloud console ("ClickOps"). It
works for a week. Then:
- nobody can say **exactly** how production is set up, or why one setting differs from staging;
- rebuilding after an outage or in a new region means remembering hundreds of clicks;
- a change has no review, no history and no undo. The audit question "who opened port 22 to the world?" has no answer.
**Infrastructure as code (IaC)** describes infrastructure in text files that live in Git. A change is a pull request: it
is reviewed, tested in CI, applied by a pipeline and recorded forever. The same files build dev, staging and production,
so they stay alike. **Terraform** (by HashiCorp, now part of IBM) and its open-source fork **OpenTofu** are the most
used IaC tools: one language (HCL) for every cloud and hundreds of SaaS products, through plugins called *providers*.
> **Tip:** In this topic the providers work on local files, random values, keys and timestamps, so everything runs
> offline on your machine. The workflow, the state, the plans and the errors are exactly the ones you meet with AWS,
> Azure or Google Cloud; the cards show the cloud versions of each idea.

steps.prompt: Production broke after "a small change" last night, made in the cloud console. Which question can a team that uses IaC answer in one minute, and a ClickOps team usually cannot?
options: Exactly what changed, who approved it and when, because every change is a reviewed commit that a pipeline applied
How much the cloud bill will be next month
Whether the cloud provider had an outage
steps.explain: History, review and repeatability are the point: `git log` on the infrastructure repo is the audit trail, and `git revert` plus a pipeline run is the undo. (Changes made in the console anyway are *drift*, which Terraform can detect: module 2.)

steps.title: Declarative, not imperative
body: An **imperative** script lists *steps*: create this, then that. Run it twice and you get two of everything, or an error.
```bash
aws s3api create-bucket --bucket shop-assets-example --region eu-west-1
aws s3api put-bucket-versioning --bucket shop-assets-example --versioning-configuration Status=Enabled
A **declarative** configuration describes the *end state*. The tool compares it with what exists and works out the
steps itself:
```hcl
resource "aws_s3_bucket" "assets" {
bucket = "shop-assets-example"
resource "aws_s3_bucket_versioning" "assets" {
bucket = aws_s3_bucket.assets.id
versioning_configuration {
status = "Enabled"
Run it a second time and Terraform says **No changes**: the result is *idempotent*. Change `status` to `"Suspended"`
and it makes exactly that one change. That comparison is the whole job of `terraform plan`.

items: A bash script that calls `aws s3api create-bucket`
A Kubernetes Deployment applied with `kubectl apply -f`
A PowerShell script that runs `New-AzResourceGroup` then `New-AzVM`
Running it twice changes nothing the second time
Running it twice fails with "already exists"
steps.explain: Declarative tools keep a model of the desired state and compute the difference. Imperative scripts are fine for one-off tasks, but they need their own checks (`if not exists ...`) to be safe to run again, and they cannot tell you what they *would* change.

steps.title: The core loop
body: | Command | What it does | Touches real infrastructure? |
| `terraform init` | downloads the providers and modules, sets up where the state lives (the *backend*) | no |
| `terraform plan` | reads what exists, compares it with your files, prints the changes it **would** make | reads only |
| `terraform apply` | makes the changes (it plans again and asks *yes* first, unless you give it a saved plan) | **yes** |
| `terraform destroy` | deletes everything this configuration manages | **yes** |
After `init` and `apply` a working folder holds:
- `.terraform/`: the downloaded providers. Never commit it.
- `.terraform.lock.hcl`: the exact provider versions and checksums. **Commit it**, like a package lock file.
- `terraform.tfstate`: Terraform's memory of what it created (module 2). With a local backend it is a file here;
at work it lives in a remote backend.
The habit that saves careers: **save the plan and apply exactly that plan.**
```bash
terraform plan -out=tfplan     # read it!
terraform apply tfplan         # applies exactly what you read, no second question

steps.prompt: Put a first run of a new configuration in order.
steps.explain: `init` first, because plan needs the providers. The last plan is the proof that the real world now matches the code. If it still shows changes, something is not idempotent (the boss of this module has that bug).

steps.title: Your first apply
prompt: `~/infra/hello/main.tf` describes a new web server's name (a `random_pet`) and its message of the day (a file in
2. Run `terraform init`. Look at what appeared: `ls -a`.
3. Save a plan with `terraform plan -out=tfplan` and read it: how many resources will be added?
4. Apply that saved plan, then show the file Terraform wrote and the output: `cat out/motd.txt`, `terraform output`.

checks.name: the providers are installed and locked
checks.fail: Run `terraform init` in `~/infra/hello` first: it installs the providers and writes `.terraform.lock.hcl`.

checks.name: both resources are in the state
checks.cmd: cd ~/infra/hello && terraform state list | sort | tr '\n' ' '
checks.fail: After the apply, `terraform state list` should show `local_file.motd` and `random_pet.server`.

checks.name: the motd names the server
checks.cmd: cd ~/infra/hello && grep -qx "Welcome to $(terraform output -raw server_name).example.com" out/motd.txt
checks.fail: `out/motd.txt` should say `Welcome to <server name>.example.com`. Did the apply finish?

checks.name: a second plan shows no changes
checks.fail: `terraform plan` should now say *No changes*. Apply the saved plan.

hints: `terraform init`, then `terraform plan -out=tfplan`. The last line says `Plan: 2 to add, 0 to change, 0 to destroy.`
`terraform apply tfplan` applies the saved plan without asking again.
steps.explain: That is the whole loop. `init` installed the two providers from the machine's offline mirror and pinned them in the lock file. The plan showed `+` for two new resources. `apply tfplan` did exactly that, and wrote what it created into `terraform.tfstate`. Run `terraform plan` once more: *No changes. Your infrastructure matches the configuration.*

steps.prompt: A teammate says: "I ran `terraform init` on the production folder by mistake. Did I change production?" What do you answer?
options: No. `init` only downloads providers and modules and connects to the backend; it never creates, changes or deletes infrastructure
Only if the lock file was missing
Yes, it refreshes the state and writes the new values back
steps.explain: `init` is safe to run any time, as often as you like. It can change the *working folder* (`.terraform/`, the lock file) and, with `-migrate-state`, copy state to a new backend, but it never calls the provider to change real objects. `plan` only reads. Only `apply`, `destroy` and some `state` and `import` commands write.

steps.title: Change the code, read the plan
body: To change infrastructure you change the files and plan again. Terraform marks each resource:
```text
+ create
~ update in-place
-/+ destroy and then create replacement
- destroy
Some attributes can be changed in place (a tag, an instance size). Others cannot: the provider must delete the object
and create a new one, and the plan marks that attribute `# forces replacement`. A `local_file`'s `content` is one of
those (a file cannot be "updated", only rewritten), just as an AWS database's `storage_encrypted` is. Replacing a
file is harmless; replacing a database deletes its data. That is why you **read every plan**.

steps.title: Change the message, keep the server
prompt: The server from the last step is running (a teammate applied `~/infra/hello`). Product wants a second line in the
1. Edit `content` in `main.tf` (`nano main.tf` opens the editor; a second line is `\n` in the string).
2. `terraform plan -out=tfplan`: which resource is replaced, and does the **server name** change?

checks.name: the motd has the maintenance line
checks.cmd: cd ~/infra/hello && diff <(printf 'Welcome to %s.example.com\nMaintenance window: Sundays 02:00 UTC\n' "$(cat /opt/dojo/state/pet)") out/motd.txt
checks.fail: `out/motd.txt` should hold exactly the two lines (the diff shows what differs). Edit `content` in `main.tf`, then plan and apply.

checks.name: the server kept its name
checks.fail: The server name changed: `random_pet.server` must not be replaced. Only change `local_file.motd`.

checks.name: the code matches the real files
checks.fail: `terraform plan` still shows changes: apply your plan.

hints: Keep `${random_pet.server.id}` in the string: that is what ties the message to the server.
The new content: `"Welcome to ${random_pet.server.id}.example.com\nMaintenance window: Sundays 02:00 UTC\n"`.
Without an editor: `sed -i 's|example.com\\n"|example.com\\nMaintenance window: Sundays 02:00 UTC\\n"|' main.tf`, then `terraform plan -out=tfplan` and `terraform apply tfplan`.
steps.explain: The plan said `-/+ local_file.motd` with `content ... # forces replacement` and left `random_pet.server` alone: Terraform only touches what changed, plus anything that depends on a value that changes. The server name lives in the state, so it is the same on every run until you replace it on purpose.

steps.prompt: Why is `terraform apply -auto-approve` (no saved plan) a bad habit on a production folder, but `terraform apply tfplan` in a pipeline is fine?
options: Without a saved plan, apply makes a new plan and runs it at once, so nobody has read what it will do; a saved plan applies exactly what was reviewed
`-auto-approve` applies to every workspace at once
steps.explain: Between your last `plan` and an unattended `apply`, a teammate may have merged something, or someone changed the real infrastructure. A saved plan file fixes the exact actions; if the state changed in the meantime, `apply tfplan` refuses with *Saved plan is stale*. CI pipelines plan on the pull request, show the plan for review, and apply that same file after the merge (module 5).
